name: Aaron Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on chat support for a banking app, the kind where everything's on your phone. Frozen cards, payments that went to the wrong person, someone in a panic because they think they've been scammed. I like the scam cases, oddly, because you can really help someone in ten minutes. What wears me out is the night shift rota, one week in four.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much do AI tools figure in your work right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI all day, every day. I'm on the pilot team for the new chatbot, which means I read its answers, flag the bad ones and write better ones for it to learn from. My boyfriend Dev teaches history at a secondary school and thinks I'm training my own replacement. He's probably right, but I'd rather be the one who understands it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, honestly, because I like this stuff. At work I'd say the pilot was useful but oversold. Online I'd post something like: turns out it's a good assistant, not a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd still have my job, and I'd be the person on the team who knows the tools best. That's worth something at review time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and ask to move from the pilot into a proper role writing the bot's answers. I'd keep putting money into my index fund every month. Maybe I'd do a short online course in data, just because I'm curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little bored. Like a film that didn't have the ending everyone promised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tools do save a bit of time, who should get that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the bank to cut the night rota, since the bot can take quiet hours. That's where saved time should go: better shifts, not fewer people. Dev says I'm naive, but it's a fair ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your job does the bot still not do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone calls and video checks for scams. A bot can freeze a card, but someone who's just lost their savings wants to hear a person. Even in the hype version, that stays human.

say: I'd say the pilot was **useful but oversold**.
I'd post that AI turned out to be **a good assistant**, not a replacement.
think: I think my job is **fine**, and knowing the tools helps at review time.
Scam victims will still **want a person**, even if the bot grows.
do: Ask to move from the pilot into **writing the bot's answers**.
Keep paying into his **index fund** every month.
Take a **short data course** online out of curiosity.
feel: He feels **calm** and a little bored by the anticlimax.
S0.quote: A bot can freeze a card, but someone who's just lost their savings wants to hear a person.
fieldNote: He's **disappointed** the hype fizzled, which is rare in this job.
He wants saved time to go on **better shifts**, not fewer people.
His boyfriend Dev calls him **naive**, a gentle tension at home.

steps.text: Apply to write the banking bot's answers full-time
Keep paying into his index fund monthly
Take a short online data course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to happen, so workers need to be in the room deciding how. Share the savings: shorter weeks, better pay, retraining. I'd post about it, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm on the right side of it for now. Someone has to tell the bot what good looks like, and I already do that. But I'd be watching friends on the team lose their jobs, and that bit doesn't sit easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard to get into the conversation design team, the people who write how the bot talks and handles tricky cases. I'd take a proper course in it, paid myself if needed, maybe eight hundred. And I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Fine for me, not fine around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mariam, who sits across from me. She's great with people but hates computers, and she's on the scam calls. I'd try to help her learn the tools, and I'd argue for her at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're helping build the thing that cuts jobs. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. I worry about that, honestly. Even conversation design shrinks once the bot gets good, and I don't know how long that is.

say: I'd say workers must be **in the room** deciding how AI comes in.
I'd argue savings should fund **shorter weeks**, better pay and retraining.
think: I think I'm on the **right side** of this change for now.
Even conversation design **shrinks** once the bot gets good.
do: Push to join the **conversation design team**, writing how the bot talks.
Pay about **eight hundred** for a proper course in conversation design.
Join the **union** and argue for colleagues like Mariam.
feel: He feels **uneasy**: fine for himself, not fine for those around him.

He's uneasy about **building the tool** that cuts colleagues' jobs.

steps.text: Apply to the bank's conversation design team
Pay for a conversation design course, about eight hundred
Join the union and speak up for Mariam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs a basic income, now, and I'd say it everywhere. If machines can do almost all thinking work, you can't leave it to each person to find a new job that doesn't exist. I'd be posting, marching, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even my job designing the bot goes in a year or two. AI that's as good as me can write its own scripts. My savings help, but I'd be one of millions in the same spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first months building stuff with the AI while it's still new, small apps, freelance work for small businesses. I'd move more savings out of shares and into cash. And I'd get properly involved in politics, a party, a campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but weirdly energised too. I'd want to be in the middle of it rather than watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Dev's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's a teacher, so hands-on in a way, kids in a room. I think schools keep teachers for a while, because parents want a person. His job might carry us, which is a funny switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long could you last on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be okay for a year or so. Ten months of costs in savings, plus the index fund. But if everyone's in trouble, the fund might be down too.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** now, everywhere I can.
I'd say you can't leave people to find **jobs that don't exist**.
think: I think even my **bot design** job goes in a year or two.
My savings help, but I'd be **one of millions** in the same spot.
do: Build **small apps and freelance** for small businesses in the first months.
Join a **party campaign** for basic income.
feel: He feels **nervous** but energised, wanting to be in the middle of it.
S2.quote: AI that's as good as me can write its own scripts.
fieldNote: He's **energised** as well as nervous, unusual among the people in this job.
He expects his partner's **teaching job** to carry the household for a while.
He worries his **index fund** falls just when he needs it.

steps.text: Freelance building small AI tools for local businesses
Move part of the index fund into cash
Join a party campaign for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build a proper safety net, so let's build it. Shorter working weeks, basic income trials, retraining money. I'd post about it constantly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd use the five years well, but I still don't know what I'd be doing in 2032. Everything I'm good at is thinking work. Five years feels like a lot until you count it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get into conversation design in the first year and earn as much as I can there. Put the extra into savings. And I'd look at training as a teacher like Dev, because teaching is part thinking, part being in a room with thirty kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, to be honest. I keep counting the years on my fingers, and the number keeps getting smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider hands-on work, since robots come later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, no. I'm not good with my hands, and I'd be starting at thirty-two. Teaching or care work, something with people, makes more sense for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dev say if you said you wanted to teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev would laugh, then help. He'd tell me teaching is harder than I think. And he'd be right.

I'd post for **shorter weeks**, basic income trials and retraining money.
think: I think everything I'm good at is **thinking work**.
I still don't know what I'd be **doing in 2032**.

Save the extra pay into his **cash savings**.
Look into **teacher training**, which mixes thinking and being in a room.
feel: He feels **anxious**, since five years feels short once counted.
S3.quote: Everything I'm good at is thinking work. Five years feels like a lot until you count it.
fieldNote: He has **no hands-on fallback** and knows it.

steps.text: Move into conversation design in the first year
Save the higher pay into cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse not to plan this as a society. I'd push for a four-day week and for a public fund to retrain people. I'd be sharing that stuff a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is enough. I'd have the bot design job for a few years, then train as a teacher. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, already in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the pilot, then conversation design, for three or four years, saving hard. Then teacher training around thirty-one. Meanwhile I'd keep the index fund going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. Uneasy about the bigger picture, but not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Won't AI come for teaching too by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching changes too, I know. AI could do the marking and lesson plans. But a room of fourteen-year-olds still needs an adult in it, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you most in this one, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who aren't like me. People who hate computers, who'd struggle to retrain. They're the ones who need the decade, and I'm not sure they'd get the help.

I'd push for a **four-day week** and a public retraining fund.

I'd be **in a classroom** by the time AGI arrives.
do: Stay in bot work **three or four years** while saving hard.
Keep paying into the **index fund** every month.
feel: He feels **mostly fine** for himself and uneasy about others.

steps.text: Keep working on the bank's bot for three or four years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2031, oddly. The fast one is so big that everyone's in it together, and maybe that forces a fix. The five-year one is long enough that politicians might do nothing and short enough that I'm left in the middle. What would help is a public retraining fund and a basic income trial, so people can take a risk on a new career.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd feel guilty. I do feel guilty, a bit, because I'm teaching the bot to do my colleague Mariam's job. I tell myself that if I didn't, someone else would. I'm not sure that makes it better.

headlineQuote: I do feel guilty, a bit, because I'm teaching the bot to do my colleague Mariam's job.
portrait: Aaron is a **27-year-old** chat agent for a banking app who uses AI every day.
He's on the **chatbot pilot team**, teaching the bot to answer like a good agent.
He's **progressive**, wants a basic income and four-day week, and lives with Dev, a teacher.
He stays calm or uneasy except in the faster AGI pictures, where he turns **anxious**.
He carries some **guilt** about training the bot that will replace colleagues.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2031 worries him most, because politicians might **do nothing** in that middle window.
whatWouldHelp: A public **retraining fund** and a **basic income** trial so people can risk a new career.
